note: Non-aligned: on cordial terms with both blocs and neither's client.
Bonn's warmth here is what makes its later push for recognition bite.

Brazil: friendly with everyone and committed to nobody. The 1980s debt crisis is what Washington means to Brasilia, so the warmth is real but thin, and the Latin American nuclear rivalry with Argentina ended at Guadalajara in 1991.

Indonesia: an anti-communist client of the West since 1965, and Japan's largest aid recipient. Relations with Beijing were suspended outright in 1967 over the coup and are only restored in August 1990 — which is why they start negative and have to be repaired.

Egypt post-Camp David: the peace with Israel is cold but eleven years old, and it bought Cairo a permanent American subsidy. The suspension from the Arab League ended in 1989 and Egypt sits with Iraq in the Arab Cooperation Council as the game opens — Cairo's turn against Baghdad in August is a choice the sim has to make, not a fact it starts with.

Israel: the American relationship is the deepest in the game. Moscow broke relations in 1967 and does not restore them until October 1991, even as it lets its Jews leave. Ankara is the one Muslim capital with full ties.

Turkey in NATO: forty years in the alliance, two million of its people working in Germany, and Incirlik. Baghdad is a customer, not a friend — the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline is Iraq's main outlet and Ozal shuts it in August 1990.
Nigeria: Commonwealth ties to London, oil ties to Washington, and the non-aligned habits of a country that has led African diplomacy since independence.

Vietnam post-Cambodia: the last troops came home in September 1989 but nothing has been forgiven. Washington's embargo is fifteen years old and has four more to run; Beijing fought a border war in 1979, kept shelling into 1988, and sank three Vietnamese ships off Johnson Reef that March. Moscow is the patron whose money stops arriving this year.

The Maghreb, eleven months after the Arab Maghreb Union was signed at Marrakesh on 17 February 1989. The treaty is real and the warmth it records is real, but it sits on top of the Western Sahara, which is why Algeria and Morocco are the one negative dyad inside it: Algeria armed and housed POLISARIO at Tindouf, the land border had been shut from 1976 to 1988, and the union is the truce rather than the settlement. Tunisia is on good terms with everyone because that has been its entire foreign policy since 1956, and its distance from Libya is the residue of the failed Djerba union of 1974 and the mass expulsion of Tunisian workers in 1985.

North Africa outward. Libya is the outlier of the period: Washington bombed Tripoli and Benghazi in April 1986, London had broken relations after WPC Yvonne Fletcher was shot from the People's Bureau in 1984, Paris had fought it by proxy in Chad until 1987, and Cairo had fought it directly in 1977 — while Moscow was the supplier of essentially the whole inventory. Algeria kept the Soviet arms relationship and the non-aligned posture it earned mediating the Algiers Accords of 1981. Morocco and Tunisia are the West's clients in the region, but scored below the NATO dyads and below Cairo's 60 with Washington: Morocco was not designated a major non-NATO ally until 2004 and Tunisia not until 2015. Rabat's quiet channel to Israel is why Morocco is the least hostile Arab capital on that row: Shimon Peres was received at Ifrane in July 1986.

Sudan seven months after Omar al-Bashir's coup. The National Islamic Front turned Khartoum toward Tehran and Baghdad and away from the Gulf patrons who had funded it under Nimeiry and Sadiq al-Mahdi; backing Iraq over Kuwait in August 1990 finished the Saudi relationship and most of the Western one. Egypt is the near neighbour that shares the river and cannot afford to lose it, and the relationship was correct in January 1990 and openly hostile within three years.
